lead: A desktop cannot execute firmware for a small microcontroller directly. The desktop is the host; the microcontroller is the target. A cross-toolchain runs on the host, translates C into target machine code, links the pieces at target addresses, and keeps symbol information for the debugger. An IDE wraps this toolchain with an editor, build buttons and a debug view. Every firmware project uses this flow: a sensor node, a motor controller, or an LPC4088 board. Some syllabi call these 'software development tools' or 'ARM development tools'.
prereq: You need Chapter 6.1 for C source and Unit 1 for flash, SRAM and memory maps.

blocks.text: The host is the computer that runs the editor and compiler; the target is the microcontroller that runs the firmware. A native compiler produces code for the host itself. A cross-compiler produces code for another instruction set. A common GCC name is arm-none-eabi-gcc: 'arm' is the target family, 'none' means no operating system, and 'eabi' is the target binary interface. Define the prefix once; every tool in the chain uses it.

The cross-compiler reads C source, checks types, expands macros, and writes assembly for the target. The assembler then converts that assembly into an object file, usually .o. The object file contains machine code, data, and a symbol table. Symbols are names such as main, UART_Init or a global variable, with their section and offset. The object file is relocatable: addresses are not final because the compiler does not know where the linker will place each section. That placement is the linker's job.

items: Compiler: C source to target assembly.
Assembler: target assembly to relocatable object.
Linker: objects and libraries to an executable.

sections.h3: Linker, linker script and memory regions

blocks.text: The linker joins object files and library code, resolves symbol references, and assigns final addresses. It follows a linker script, a text file with two main parts. MEMORY declares the target memory regions: flash from 0x00000000, size 256 KB; SRAM from 0x20000000, size 64 KB. SECTIONS says which input sections go into which region. Common output sections are .text for code and constants, .data for initialised variables, and .bss for zero-initialised variables.

Flash holds .text and the initial values of .data. RAM holds .data after the startup code copies the values from flash, plus .bss after startup zeroes it. Startup code sets the stack pointer where the architecture requires it, copies .data, zeroes .bss, and jumps to main. It is written in assembly or C with a special section name, and the vector table points to its reset handler. Stack and heap live in RAM and must be reserved in the linker script.

After linking, the map file lists every section and symbol with addresses and sizes. Read it to check that flash and RAM are not overfull. The linker does not run on the target; it only prepares the image.

sections.h3: ELF, HEX, BIN, libraries, make and the IDE

blocks.text: The linker writes an ELF file. ELF is Executable and Linkable Format; it holds code, data, section addresses and symbols. A HEX file, such as Intel HEX, is ASCII records of bytes and addresses for programmers that cannot use ELF. A BIN file is a raw memory image with no address or symbol information. Debuggers prefer ELF because source lines and variable names are present.

Library code is stored in archives, often .a files, and the linker pulls only the object files needed. The C library may be newlib or a smaller embedded variant. A makefile lists source files, flags and output names, and rebuilds only what changed. An IDE supplies an editor, project settings, a build button and a debugger front end; under the button it runs make or an equivalent builder. The IDE is convenience, not a separate compiler.

An in-system programmer writes the image into the target flash while the chip stays on the board. Many microcontrollers have a ROM bootloader that accepts data over UART, USB or CAN. On an LPC4088-style part, holding a boot pin and using the vendor ISP tool is one example. Other boards use JTAG or SWD pods. The connection needs correct target voltage, ground and clock; a wrong adapter setting gives 'no target' errors.

A debugger connects to the target's debug port, halts the CPU, reads registers and memory, sets breakpoints and single-steps. For source-level debugging it loads the ELF file so addresses map back to C lines and variable names. It can also program flash through the same connection. The debugger is not the same as a simulator; a simulator runs on the host with no board. See Chapter 6.3 for that trade-off.

figure.caption: The C source becomes a relocatable object, then a linked ELF or HEX; the linker script decides target addresses. Notice the debugger reads the linked file and its symbols.

spec.title: Cross-toolchain flow
spec.aria: A C source file passes through a cross-compiler, assembler and linker into an ELF or HEX file that the debugger loads.

examples.question: A microcontroller has 256 KB flash starting at 0x00000000 and 64 KB SRAM starting at 0x20000000. A program has .text 40 KB, .data 8 KB and .bss 12 KB. The stack and heap are not included in these figures. Does the program fit? State what goes in flash and in RAM, and the free space in each.
steps: Flash holds .text and the initial values of .data: 40 KB + 8 KB = 48 KB.
RAM holds .data after copying and .bss after zeroing: 8 KB + 12 KB = 20 KB.
Both 48 KB ≤ 256 KB and 20 KB ≤ 64 KB, so it fits. Reserve part of the 44 KB free RAM for stack and heap.
examples.answer: The image uses 48 KB of flash and 20 KB of RAM, leaving 208 KB flash and 44 KB RAM free; it fits.
examples.check:
text_kb = 40
data_kb = 8
bss_kb = 12
flash_kb = 256
ram_kb = 64
flash_used = text_kb + data_kb
ram_used = data_kb + bss_kb
flash_free = flash_kb - flash_used
ram_free = ram_kb - ram_used
print(flash_used)
print(ram_used)
print(flash_free)
print(ram_free)

traps: Putting .data only in RAM and forgetting that its initial values occupy flash; startup code copies them.
Counting .bss in flash. .bss has no stored bytes; startup code zeroes RAM.
Ignoring stack and heap in the RAM budget, then calling a 64 KB RAM part full at 60 KB of .data plus .bss.
Treating a BIN file as if it contained addresses and symbols; ELF and HEX carry address information.
Thinking the linker script is executed by the target; it is read by the host linker.

quiz.a: A compiler that runs on a host but produces machine code for a different target instruction set.

quiz.q: Why does an initialised global variable use both flash and RAM?
quiz.a: Its initial value is stored in flash in .data; startup code copies it to RAM so the program can change it.

quiz.q: Flash is 128 KB, RAM is 32 KB. .text = 50 KB, .data = 6 KB and .bss = 10 KB. Find flash used, RAM used and the free space in each.
quiz.a: Flash used 50 + 6 = 56 KB, free 72 KB. RAM used 6 + 10 = 16 KB, free 16 KB. It fits.

quiz.q: A build links without error but the board resets continuously. The map file shows .bss ends at 0x2000FFF0 and the stack starts at 0x2000FFF0. What is the likely problem?
quiz.a: No RAM gap is left for the stack; the stack collides with .bss. Increase RAM, reduce .bss, or reserve stack space correctly.

quiz.q: Name three common output formats and one use of each.
quiz.a: ELF for debugging and symbols; HEX for programmers; BIN for raw flash images.

quiz.q: What does a map file tell you?
quiz.a: Section and symbol addresses and sizes after linking; it is used to check flash and RAM budgets.

quiz.q: A linker script gives .data a run address at 0x20000000 and a load address in flash. What does startup code do with .data?
quiz.a: It copies the initial values from the flash load address to the RAM run address before main runs.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production teams wrap the same toolchain in CMake, Ninja and CI jobs that fail a build when the map file crosses a size budget. LLVM/Clang toolchains are common alongside GCC, and container images pin exact compiler versions. Hardware trace and instruction trace probes extend debugging beyond breakpoints. Search for 'GNU Arm Embedded Toolchain', 'linker script MEMORY SECTIONS' and 'SWD debugging' to go deeper.
